When Rain visits the town of Felicitas in Final Fantasy Resonance, he meets an old acquaintance in the form of "Auntie Chloe". Chloe - herself a guest vision in FF Brave Exvius - is a trusted scholar in the employ of Grandshelt, recently tasked with investigating the kingdom's crystals. The lands surrounding Felicitas bear the highest concentration of buried crystals, so Chloe has opted to begin by studying the regional sediments. She asks for Rain's help in collecting various samples from the ground.

In classical mythology, 'Chloe' is one of the common monikers of the goddess Demeter, patron of agriculture, the harvesting of crops, and fertility. She is the mother of Persephone and is said to have searched for her daughter after the latter was taken to the underworld by Hades, king of the dead. The ancient Greeks eventually called Hades 'Plouton', the ‘Wealthy One’, because they were afraid to speak his name aloud. The wealth in question was the precious minerals and gemstones that could be mined within the earth. Resonance's Felicitas - itself a mining town - shares a name with the Roman goddess of agricultural fertility, prosperity, and good fortune. 

It's therefore unlikely to be a coincidence that it is Chloe who is investigating buried crystals and who sends Rain in search of samples from the rich earth around Felicitas. And that doesn't even touch on the events at Kobolos...

WHY ARE CENTRAL BANKS PULLING THEIR GOLD BACK HOME?  

Bravos Research explains in an excellent video why Central banks are quietly shifting hundreds of tons of gold out of New York and overseas vaults and back under closer control. Dutch, French, and Indian institutions have moved massive amounts in recent years while stock markets sit near records. The official explanations sound technical, yet the scale, speed, and timing point to preparation for something far larger than most people realize.

THE SUDDEN GOLD MOVES  
➡️ Just last month the Dutch Central Bank moved 78 tons of gold out of New York and Ottawa into the Bank of England in London.  
➡️ France revealed earlier this year that it sold all 129 tons of gold it kept in New York and bought the same amount back in Europe.  
➡️ India has quietly brought home almost 380 tons of gold in just three years.  
➡️ According to the World Gold Council’s latest survey the share of central banks that have moved more of their gold home has almost doubled since last year.  
➡️ The share that are now spreading holdings across more overseas vaults has jumped fivefold.

THE OFFICIAL LANGUAGE  
➡️ The Dutch Central Bank said the move improves the tradability of its reserves and allows it to be better prepared for a severe crisis.  
➡️ That is not language a central bank uses lightly.  
➡️ In July the European Central Bank changed its enhanced euro facility after Christine Lagarde warned that financial market stress is likely to become more frequent.  
➡️ The ECB wants to avoid that stress triggering fire sales in global funding markets.

THE BLUEPRINT FROM BASEL  
➡️ The Bank for International Settlements published a report last year outlining what it calls the next generation monetary and financial system.  
➡️ The word that appears countless times is elasticity.  
➡️ The Federal Reserve Act of 1913 created the Fed to furnish an elastic currency after the Panic of 1907.  
➡️ Elasticity means expanding the supply of money when the system needs liquidity and scaling it back when conditions normalize.  
➡️ Liquidity is the oxygen of the financial system: invisible when present, suffocating when it disappears.

THE REPEATING PATTERN  
➡️ Liquidity crises struck in 1929, 1974, 1987, 2001, 2008, and 2020 for the same core reason: a sudden lack of liquidity.  
➡️ The IMF’s latest financial stability report states that risks are high and underlying vulnerabilities could be exposed in a crisis.  
➡️ Just last month the Federal Reserve raised its interest rate for the first time since 2023, with markets expecting further hikes.  
➡️ Nine out of ten major central banks are raising rates in 2026, a coordinated global tightening.

THE 1920s RHYME  
➡️ At Davos earlier this year Larry Fink, Ken Griffin, and Christine Lagarde compared the 2020s to the 1920s.  
➡️ Lagarde likened today’s AI revolution to the electricity and assembly lines of that era while noting the stock market was doing extremely well.  
➡️ The 1920s boom, fueled by technological optimism, produced leverage, stretched valuations, and a vulnerable system that cracked when conditions reversed.  
➡️ Overlaying today’s stock market on the 1920s produces an almost exact replica, this time driven by AI rather than electricity.  
➡️ The IMF highlights valuation risks, the potential for an AI-driven correction, rising leverage, and circular financing schemes that heighten the risk of forced selling.  
➡️ The BIS warns that financing of AI is increasingly leveraged and concentrated.

WHY MOVE THE GOLD NOW  
➡️ Central banks are tightening the very conditions that can trigger a liquidity crisis while preparing the tools to respond.  
➡️ History shows interventions grow larger and faster with each crisis: the 2008 response was massive, the pandemic response even bigger.  
➡️ Gold reserves serve as collateral for the extra cash needed to inject liquidity at scale.  
➡️ The more gold they hold and the more easily they can access it, the more room they have to respond.

THE TIMING WINDOW  
➡️ In the 1920s the Fed began raising rates in early 1928 yet the stock market continued rising for another year and a half.  
➡️ The same window appears open today: rates have only just started rising and their full impact may take roughly a year.  
➡️ Optimism around AI can still drive strong returns in the meantime before the stretch reverses.

THE BOTTOM LINE  
Central banks are not moving gold because everything is fine. They are positioning reserves for tradability and collateral ahead of a liquidity squeeze that rhymes with the end of the roaring twenties, even as stock markets ignore the signal and keep climbing.  
The gold is coming home because the people who control the system already see the oxygen running thin.

🇺🇲 🇷🇺 🇪🇺 Trump is offering Moscow things Europe controls: ECFR's Demarais and O'Brien say the EU holds the keys to Russia's frozen reserves, Lukoil's refineries and Nord Stream

Washington's sweeteners for Moscow depend on assets that sit in Europe, argue Agathe Demarais and Jim O'Brien of the European Council on Foreign Relations. They list what US envoys have floated in recent weeks: access to part of the Russian central bank reserves that European governments immobilised in 2022, the sale of Lukoil's foreign business to investors close to the envoys, and talks on selling Gazprom's stake in the Nord Stream pipeline to an American company. 

They add that on Oct. 9 President Trump allowed US firms to import Russian diesel, and seven days later waived part of the new sanctions in the Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act that Congress passed in September. 

⚠️ Their verdict: "many of the things that Trump is offering Moscow are not Washington's to give."

The authors concede that Europe looks like a bystander. Lukoil is on the US sanctions list and off the EU's, so only the US Treasury sets the terms of a sale. EU sanctions bar European firms from Nord Stream business but do not stop Gazprom from selling its 51% stake to an American buyer. On Serbia's NIS refinery, they write, Washington has set every deadline, while Gazprom Neft trimmed its stake to just under the 50% threshold that would trigger EU measures.

Their case is that geography is leverage. The EU renewed its own Russia sanctions in June for 12 months. Euroclear, a Belgian firm under EU law, holds the bulk of the roughly $300 billion in immobilised Russian reserves. Lukoil's foreign assets include the Burgas refinery in Bulgaria, Petrotel in Romania, a stake in the Zeeland refinery in the Netherlands and Finland's Teboil chain, and Nord Stream lands in Germany. 

Demarais and O'Brien propose three moves: require EU approval for sales of Russian-owned energy assets on EU soil, tied to Russian concessions; fix a firm end date for Russian pipeline gas, now set for September 2027, which would make a Nord Stream stake worth little; and answer Washington on the reserves with a claims tally. They cite the World Bank's $588 billion estimate of Ukraine's reconstruction needs and Kyiv School of Economics estimates of more than $170 billion in Western corporate losses in Russia, and conclude that Russia's liabilities are more than twice its immobilised assets.

They flag the costs. Trump could retaliate, including with Graham act tariffs on buyers of Russian energy. Sanctioning Lukoil needs all 27 EU members, though national investment screens do not, and Slovakia and Hungary asked Brussels on Oct. 19 for flexibility on the gas deadline. 

The piece is a reminder that the administration's Russia offers can be blocked in Brussels, and the authors note that a Democratic Congress after Nov. 3 could add investigations. 

Source: Trump’s Russia deals are not his to make: https://t.co/Rt3SBWiSNY via @ecfr

The index tracks hourly rental rates for five NVIDIA GPUs at fixed weights: H100 40%, B200 25%, H200 15%, A100 10%, and RTX 4090 10%. This converts fragmented GPU rental pricing into one tradable benchmark. AI developers can hedge rising training and inference costs while providers can manage revenue risk without relying on bilateral deals. 

It sits next to Injective’s existing pre-IPO perps for companies like OpenAI and Anthropic, so the same venue now covers both the model builders and the infrastructure powering them.

The practical test is whether open interest concentrates on the higher-weight datacenter GPUs once desks start using it for inventory management, or whether flow spreads across the full basket including the consumer 4090.

📝 New article on Our World in Data: How much development aid is spent on climate change?

For a long time, we didn’t have good data to answer this basic question. But using tags from the RioMarkers database, we’ve constructed a dataset on how much aid is spent on climate change, and what that funding is used for.

The headline result is that, in 2024, around one-fifth of development aid was climate-related. For allocable bilateral aid — that is, aid given from one country to another for specific projects — the share was one-third.

Some of that aid is given to climate mitigation projects, which aim to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Some is given to adaptation: ways of dealing with the impacts of climate change. And just as much is given to projects that do both.

Whether climate-related aid is in conflict or crowds out other aid efforts is hard to untangle. When we look at individual examples, many look like traditional aid projects, with a subtle link to climate efforts. Take the building of a hospital in Tanzania; its main objective is to provide healthcare and save lives. But it’s also tagged as a climate-related project because it was built with energy efficiency in mind. Would that hospital have been built in a world without climate change? Probably.

Other cases are less clear. Concerns about the displacement of traditional projects seem real, but so too are concerns that commitments to climate finance are often met through a relabeling exercise.

In our article, we dig into the data on climate-related aid projects: how it’s changed over time and which countries give and receive it.

$IREN: Its Real Competitive Advantage Is Taking Shape

The strongest competitive advantage in the AI era is neither superior hardware nor superior software, but the ability to optimize hardware and software together.

The market is still taking a rather crude approach, lumping a wide range of companies together under a single concept. Traditional cloud computing is software-driven, and software development follows the principle of abstraction because differences in underlying hardware performance are relatively small. But AI computing clusters, particularly massive clusters comprising tens or even hundreds of thousands of GPUs, have shattered that abstraction.

For a cloud service provider to gain a genuine competitive advantage in the AI era, building a closed loop of deep hardware control and precise software coordination is one path to establishing substantial differentiation. If a cloud provider lacks sufficient control over its hardware, its software capabilities may not translate into actual performance, or it may be unable to receive the feedback it needs. Therefore, the optimal approach should involve:

Bottom-up feedback: hardware informing software. Physical infrastructure feeds real-time information about power-distribution bottlenecks, network congestion, and node-failure warnings into the cloud-native software orchestration layer.

Top-down control: software adjusting hardware behavior. Based on the priorities of training and inference workloads, software dynamically adjusts power allocation across the cluster, partitions computing resources, and coordinates data storage with GPU scheduling.

This also includes capabilities that require close hardware-software collaboration, such as hardware-level multi-tenancy, network and switch isolation, and physical and logical GPU slicing technologies.

These technical requirements are precisely why new companies have an opportunity to compete on equal footing with established cloud giants in this industry. Software strength alone is not enough, and neither is the hardware strength of traditional cloud providers. In this new era, companies will have a chance to emerge as winners only if they excel at optimizing both hardware and software in coordination.

The AI industry is still in its early stages, and AI infrastructure is still taking shape. The concept of the neocloud remains extremely vague. Does bare metal have the advantage? Does software have the advantage? Neither, on its own. Of course, the market is enormous, and for a considerable period, there will be room for many players to survive. But to become truly competitive in this industry, a company must be strong in both software and hardware coordination.

Infrastructure is undergoing enormous changes. Companies deeply involved in building this new infrastructure will gain advantages in physical facilities. The software capabilities developed on top of that foundation will gradually take shape, purpose-built for the new hardware infrastructure. As a result, they should perform exceptionally well in coordinating increasingly complex systems. I have already seen this trend emerging at the recent GTC conference in Berlin, and it has also been validated by several software capabilities NVIDIA recently developed in collaboration with IREN.

This year, the market has viewed NBIS as having this potential and awarded it a high valuation. NBIS wants to build an integrated, self-contained system, placing particular emphasis on its full-stack software capabilities. However, it cannot match IREN in the scale and depth of its infrastructure deployment. This gap will become increasingly apparent over time, particularly when it comes to individual gigawatt-scale sites. Leasing can make it relatively easy to secure numerous smaller sites quickly, but sites exceeding 300 MW are much harder to secure. Gigawatt-scale sites are effectively out of reach for a leasing-based model.

IREN is building a flagship AI factory for NVIDIA's DSX system. There will be many things that only IREN is positioned to undertake, such as developing individual gigawatt-scale sites, clusters of multiple gigawatt-scale sites located in close proximity, and sophisticated interactions with the power grid. IREN and NVIDIA could well develop multiple reference configurations at different megawatt scales for the market to choose from, ranging from small sites to hyperscale facilities. Throughout this process, IREN is participating extensively in the standardization of AI infrastructure, giving it a strong first-mover advantage in physical infrastructure.

On this foundation, the cloud technology team IREN is assembling will play a critical role, developing software optimized to interact and coordinate with the new AI infrastructure. Throughout this process, its vertically integrated model will prove enormously valuable.

Competition has never been about winning at a single point; it is a massive exercise in system-wide coordination. Even Elon Musk appears underprepared in this regard. His approach of scrambling to pile computing capacity onto gas turbines as quickly as possible may resemble a peacock spreading its feathers: everyone sees the impressive display at the front, but no one notices what is going on behind it. In my view, regardless of whether he can actually pull it off, even if he succeeds, the economics of this approach will likely be very poor. Tesla was built around an uncompromising focus on cost efficiency, but when it comes to AI, that philosophy seems to have turned into spending whatever it takes. I am not convinced by this approach.

As my research has deepened recently, I have come to understand more and more of the decisions IREN has made over the past year. IREN is a deeply involved builder of the AI infrastructure that is now taking shape. By collaborating with leading companies in the AI industry, it is positioning itself as a leader in physical infrastructure, while building a powerful software ecosystem for optimization and coordination on top of that foundation.

For multiple years, I spent the majority of my time focused on the transparency of frontier AI companies. When I was working on that topic, many people asked me why I prioritized this issue. 

Those skeptical of substantial regulation often asked because they believed it was unnecessary. Those supportive of substantive regulation often asked because they believed it was insufficient. For now, I don't want to re-litigate this issue but make a simpler point based on today's events.

The Anthropic S-1 is a wonderful example of the value of  (in this case mandated) transparency into frontier AI companies. It is dispositive on the financial health not just of this one important company, but the industry's financial health, the prospects for its future, and the even broader risks and opportunities society will contend with if/as frontier AI advances forward. 

It should make us think deeply about what disclosures from frontier AI companies will be valuable, and how those disclosures will come to be, especially when the institutional apparatus of the SEC and the federal laws for US corporate finance does not (yet) exist.

CoWoS 最大で20％値上げへ
これ本当だったら、来年の先端パッケージング売り上げはどえらいことになる

TSMCのCoWoSは、価格を最大20％引き上げると報じられている。
包装におけるリードタイムの​​長期化と生産能力の逼迫は、機器製造に影響を与えており、サプライチェーン全体が納期の確保と生産拡大のために奔走している。

AIチップの生産能力確保をめぐる争奪戦により、高度なパッケージングの価格が高騰している。サプライチェーン関係者によると、TSMCのCoWoS価格は再び値上げされる見込みで、最大20%に達する可能性があるという。一部のパッケージング部品のリードタイムは既に延長されており、生産能力の逼迫による圧力はますます強まっている。この生産能力確保の動きは、機器業界にも波及している。業界関係者によると、顧客はもはや価格交渉に応じず、納期さえ約束されれば発注するとのことだ。機器のリードタイムは最長8ヶ月にまで延長されており、サプライチェーンは供給と生産拡大に奔走している。

高度なパッケージングに対する需要は、AI GPUからサーバーCPU、カスタムASICへと広がり、未充足の注文は増加の一途を辿っている。半導体メーカー各社は、AIチップのテスト期間の長期化がパッケージングとテストの両方の能力に負担をかけていると指摘している。ウェハーファウンドリやOSAT（半導体組立・テスト外注）企業は、CoWoS（協力・テスト）価格の新たな調整局面に備えており、価格は10～20％上昇すると見込まれている。

機器メーカー各社は、TSMCが毎年実施している機器調達において、以前は価格交渉や同一価格での追加機能の要求をしていたことを明らかにした。しかし、今年は再交渉は行われず、追加機能なしで当初の価格で機器が調達された。過去数年と比べて、サプライヤーに対する価格引き下げや機能追加の圧力は軽減され、受注収益性の維持に役立っている。

半導体メーカー各社によると、顧客は納期を最優先事項としており、装置のリードタイムは3～6ヶ月から6～8ヶ月に延びている。需要の増加に伴い、上流工程の加工業者や部品サプライヤーは生産能力の逼迫に直面しており、短期的には大幅な拡張は難しい状況だ。装置は納期通りに納入する必要があり、新たな生産能力の解放速度は依然としてサプライチェーンの供給能力に左右される。

設備メーカーは、生産能力拡大の速度は工程上のボトルネックによって左右されると指摘している。最新鋭のパッケージング工場が着工からボトルネック箇所でのフル稼働に至るまでには、およそ3年かかるとされている。実際の生産量は、リソグラフィ、現像、ダイボンディングなどの工程の処理能力によって左右される。工程調整に伴い、ボトルネックは移動する。工場が完成し、設備が設置された後も、安定供給を開始する前に、校正と検証が必要となる。

TSMCの会長であるC.C. Wei氏は、最近の決算説明会で、CoWoSは依然として顧客にとって最適な選択肢であると述べました。現在、5倍サイズのマスクパッケージは優れた歩留まりで量産体制に入っており、同社は9倍および14倍サイズのマスクソリューションの開発を継続するとともに、CoPoS技術を進歩させ、将来の大型パッケージング需要とコスト削減に対応していきます。

AIチップは、より多くの演算チップと高帯域幅メモリ（HBM）を統合するため、パッケージング面積と製造工程の複雑さが増大する。装置メーカーは以前から、チップサイズの大型化は装置の時間当たりの生産量を減少させると指摘してきた。チップの数が変わらなくても、顧客は装置の追加を必要とする可能性があり、生産能力拡張への需要をさらに高めることになるだろう。

TSMCは引き続き先進パッケージング能力の増強を進めている。アナリストは、同社のCoWoSの月間生産能力が2026年までに13万枚以上、2027年までに20万枚に達すると予測している。工場開発計画には、嘉義にあるAP7工場の段階的な建設、台南にあるAP8 P2工場への設備設置、そして先進パッケージング需要に対応するためのAP6工場におけるSoIC（So-IC）生産能力の拡張などが含まれる。海外では、TSMCは2028年に米国にあるAP1先進パッケージング工場での生産開始を計画している。

BREAKING $AMD | $TSM CoWoS advanced packaging prices are reportedly set to rise by up to 20% amid tight capacity driven by surging AI demand.

Zhang Jiarui in Taiwan’s Commercial Times, reports that TSMC is preparing another round of CoWoS (Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate) price increases of roughly 10–20%. This follows strong demand that has already extended some packaging lead times and kept capacity under pressure.

Demand drivers
Capacity constraints originally centered on AI GPUs are spreading to server CPUs and custom ASICs. Unmet orders continue to grow. Longer test times for AI chips are simultaneously stressing packaging and testing capacity at both foundries and OSAT (outsourced semiconductor assembly and test) firms.

Pricing and customer behavior
Supply-chain sources say TSMC’s CoWoS quotes are under upward pressure. Equipment customers are prioritizing delivery over price; many are no longer negotiating and will place orders as long as lead times can be met. TSMC itself has not reopened price negotiations for equipment this year and is purchasing at existing prices without demanding extra features easing margin pressure on suppliers.

Lead times and bottlenecks
Equipment delivery has stretched from the previous 3–6 months to 6–8 months. Upstream components and processing capacity are tight and hard to expand quickly. Building a new advanced-packaging plant from groundbreaking to full loading of bottleneck stations takes about three years. Bottlenecks shift among process steps such as lithography, development, and die bonding; even after equipment is installed, calibration and qualification are required before stable output.

TSMC’s technology and capacity plans
Chairman C.C. Wei has stated that CoWoS remains customers’ preferred solution. Five times reticle size packaging is already in volume production with strong yields. TSMC is developing nine  and fourteen times reticle size options and advancing CoPoS technology for larger packages and lower cost. Broader AI chips that integrate more compute dies plus HBM (high-bandwidth memory) increase package area and complexity; larger dies also reduce equipment throughput, which can further raise the number of tools required.

Capacity targets
Institutional estimates point to CoWoS monthly capacity exceeding 130,000 wafers in 2026 and double in 2027. Expansion includes phased work at Chiayi AP7, equipment installation at Tainan AP8 P2, SoIC capacity growth at AP6, and a planned U.S. AP1 advanced-packaging plant targeted for production in 2028.

Animals and plants use conceptually similar immune systems to detect microbes and activate defenses. In both lineages, pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) perceive pathogen- or microbe-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs or MAMPs) and host-derived damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs). 

Whereas animals rely on specialized immune cells, plants harness individual cells expressing diverse PRRs. In the apoplast, which lies outside the plasma membrane and includes the cell wall, PRRs detect immunogenic fragments released from microbial proteins by plant hydrolytic enzymes. Conversely, pathogen-secreted enzymes can degrade constituents of the apoplast, generating DAMPs that activate immunity. 

In three new Science papers, researchers report expansions of this surveillance, revealing receptor architectures and mechanisms that enable plants to discriminate immunogenic carbohydrates. The findings illustrate how ligand specificity and receptor assembly confine immune activation to the context of microbial challenge.

A team in Cuttack has shown that an AI-designed enzyme can edit rice DNA in several different ways. They also regenerated edited plants and grew them to maturity.

The original enzyme came from Profluent Bio, an American company. The Indian work was adapting it for rice and testing what it could actually do inside a crop.

Profluent trained a large language model on over a million natural CRISPR systems to generate OpenCRISPR-1, a new DNA-cutting protein. The team at ICAR-Central Rice Research Institute, led by Dr Kutubuddin A. Molla, adapted it for rice cells. Their version is called POC1.

ICAR describes this as the 1st demonstration of an AI-designed nuclease working in plant cells. Priya Das and Romio Saha are the co-first authors.

Why does this matter?

An AI-generated protein sequence still has to work inside a living cell. Here, the Cuttack team showed that the adapted protein could support several editing methods in rice. Other plant researchers now have another experimentally tested tool to work with; the team has deposited its constructs with Addgene.

That could help researchers develop and test useful crop traits. It does not, by itself, establish better yields or a variety ready for farmers.

The paper was published in New Phytologist in May. ICAR's announcement came on 21 October.

P.S. A nuclease is a protein that cuts DNA. Base editing changes individual DNA letters; prime editing can rewrite a short stretch.

Bharat is rising. 🙏🙏

Sources: Das et al., New Phytologist, 2026; Ruffolo et al., Nature, 2025; ICAR, 21 October 2026.

He has a point. To me the OpenAI announcement seems to be about mathematical physics.

To most people "mathematical physics" and "theoretical physics" sound interchangeable but they are different disciples.

Theoretical physics is solidly part of physics. In this area, researchers develop either theories that explain observations already made, or they improve existing theories to make predictions for observations. (At least that's what they should be doing.)

Mathematical physics on the other hand is usually part of the department of mathematics, not physics. It is concerned, loosely speaking, with cleaning up the mess that physicists have made of their theories of nature. Or in some cases studying the properties of theories that have nothing to do with nature. (Like physics in lower or higher dimensions, fields that don't exist in nature, etc.)

People in these two disciplines work closely together of course. But mathematical physics is more maths than physics. I would not consider it part of the natural sciences as it is not itself concerned with describing nature. 

I don't know exactly what the OpenAI discovery is about, but it sounds like it is more in the area mathematical physics rather than theoretical physics. I am not saying this makes it irrelevant, but as Andreas points out, it is of limited interest for applications.

In China, more than one in five workers is still employed in agriculture.

China makes and exports more goods than any other country. So, perhaps unsurprisingly, when we think about China’s economy, the first thing that comes to mind is often manufacturing — increasingly at the technological frontier in electric vehicles, batteries, and solar panels.

China’s position in manufacturing follows decades of economic transformation. The chart shows one aspect of this: the decline in agricultural employment.

At the turn of the 21st century, around half of all Chinese workers were employed in agriculture. One generation later, that share had more than halved, reaching 22% in 2025.

It's striking how far the share of workers in agriculture has fallen, and just as striking how high it remains. Agriculture employs more than a fifth of China’s workers, while accounting for less than 7% of its GDP.

(written by @EOrtizOspina)

A 2024 study detected microplastics in 100% of human and dog testicular tissue.

In another study, microplastics were detected in the semen and urine of all of 113 tested men from China.

Researchers broke down plastic type and how they affected sperm quality.

The most common came from packaging (polystyrene, polypropylene, and polyethylene).

PTFE, the synthetic polymer used in non-stick Teflon pans, proved the most lethal, creating 11% lower sperm concentration and 9% fewer total sperm.

Ten studies have measured microplastics in human semen. Five found 100% detection.

The rest from 84% down to 37%, but older tests used standard infrared microscopes that are blind to particles smaller than 10–20 microns. Newer studies used Raman spectroscopy, which can spot particles down to 1 micron.

So in short, 100% prevalence is plausible if not likely.

Americans have already staked more than $1.4 billion on prediction markets tied to the outcome of this year's U.S. midterm elections, and that figure is expected to exceed $2 billion by election day.

Millions of voters, alongside major trading firms and private companies, will trade on these markets—a boom that has provoked strong opposition from Democratic Party leaders, state governments, and much of the electorate.

"At issue are two questions: one of legality and one of prudence," writes @SamHenryLazarus in a new CFR report. "The first is whether election markets are legal to begin with—specifically, if they qualify as 'swaps' under federal commodities law and can therefore be offered nationwide. The second is whether the utility of election markets outweighs the risks they pose to the United States’ moral fabric, democratic process, and financial markets."

Election markets hold significant potential as tools for political forecasting, but only if policymakers take steps to control for insider trading and improve oversight, he argues.

Reform would serve both opponents and advocates of election markets, Lazarus argues. “Inaction will serve neither camp: scandals will abound, trust in the democratic process will erode, and traders will be defrauded.”

$PRME | FDA proposes adding new gene variants to an approved editing BLA without new clinical trials 🚨

On October 27, 2026, FDA's Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research issued a draft guidance, "Individualized Human Genome Editing Products: Considerations for BLA Submission and Postapproval Management".

It covers monogenic diseases where patients carry different pathogenic variants in the same gene. A single BLA under section 351(a) of the PHS Act can hold multiple product variants, each tailored to one mutation, bounded by a concept the guidance introduces: the individualized feature space, or IFS, the declared limits within which the editing components may vary.

Strength, formulation, the in vivo delivery vehicle such as the lipid nanoparticle, and the ex vivo cell type should remain constant across variants. What varies is typically the guide RNA. A variant falling inside the established IFS counts as a manufacturing change rather than a new product, submitted as a BLA supplement with in vitro activity data showing on-target editing at or above a clinically established threshold, plus NGS-based on-target and off-target safety data for each guide and editor combination. Where the link between in vitro data and clinical safety and effectiveness is well understood, FDA generally does not expect clinical data for those additions, and recommends an approved postapproval change management protocol under 21 CFR 601.12(e). Widening the IFS requires a prior approval supplement, and validation designed to cover the full IFS generally avoids revalidating per variant.

Prime Medicine's liver franchise is built on that architecture. The universal liver LNP holds formulation, GalNAc targeting ligand and prime editor mRNA constant and swaps only the guide RNAs, the same split FDA draws between fixed elements and variable features. PM577a targets ATP7B H1069Q, roughly 30 to 50 percent of Wilson disease alleles in the United States and Europe, with the first patient dosed in October 2026 and a follow-on R778L candidate in preclinical development. Those additional ATP7B variants could reach the label as supplements to the same application rather than as separate programs, sharply lowering the marginal cost of each additional mutation.

Three things set the ceiling. The IFS should be supported primarily by clinical data, and the applicant should justify that the variants actually studied span the entire proposed space, with extrapolation judged case by case on natural history, genotype-phenotype associations and genotype-driven safety factors, including variants producing no protein, where immunogenicity risk may rise. One studied variant supports a narrow space, not an open one. The framework also scales within a single gene and a single editing outcome, so the Wilson disease franchise and the SERPINA1 program behind PM647 would not share an IFS. And FDA's worked example varies a single guide RNA spacer, while a pegRNA varies across spacer, primer binding site and RT template, with a nicking guide alongside, so how wide a space that supports is unsettled.

The mechanism line falls where prime editing sits. Without naming it, FDA states that an editor relying on a reverse transcriptase does not belong in the same BLA as a base editor, since off-target and immunogenicity risks differ, and that adding one to an approved base editing product would be a new product requiring a new BLA. RT-based editing is treated as its own mechanistic class, which bounds what can later be folded into one application and equally keeps base editing BLAs from absorbing prime editors.

And the US share keeps growing. It acquired around 60% of new compute each year from 2022 to 2024, then 72% in 2025, and 78% in the first half of 2026.

This data comes from our interactive AI Chip Imports explorer, which estimates and visualizes national compute shares using customs records.

It’s the latest piece in our project to map the AI chip supply chain, which also provides data on the components used to manufacture chips, sales volumes, the data centers that house chips, and the companies that own and use them.
